title: Statistics
body:
Statistics covers reasoning from a sample to the population it came from. Measuring every
member of a population is usually impossible, so a conclusion is drawn from a subset, and the
subset is never exactly like the whole. Quantifying how far off it might be is what the course
does, and it is why no result here is reported as a bare number: every estimate arrives with a
second number saying how much to trust it.

The blocks run in one direction and each depends on the one before it. Describe a sample with
[[Descriptive Statistics]]. Model the mechanism that produced it with [[Probability]],
[[Random Variable]] and [[Probability Distribution]]. Work out how a statistic computed from
one sample behaves across all the samples that were never drawn, using
[[Sampling Distribution]] and the [[Central Limit Theorem]]. Only then make claims, with
[[Confidence Interval]], [[Hypothesis Testing]] and [[Linear Regression]].

[[CALCULUS 1]] is a working prerequisite, because a continuous random variable is defined by
an [[Integral]] and a probability is an area under a curve. For this vault the course is also
the bridge into machine learning: [[Type I and Type II Errors]] is the [[Confusion Matrix]]
that fourth-year computer science uses under different names.

## Topics

### Describing a sample

A statistic is computed from a sample and a parameter describes the population, so $\bar{x}$
estimates $\mu$, $s$ estimates $\sigma$, and $\hat{p}$ estimates $p$. Roman letters mark what
was measured and Greek letters mark what it estimates, and keeping that straight is what makes
every later formula readable.

[[Average Value]] indexes the three measures of centre, on the data $2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9$:

```
mean   = 40 / 8 = 5      uses every value, so one outlier moves it
median = 4.5             the middle, unaffected by how extreme the tails are
mode   = 4               most frequent, and the only one that works on categories
```

All three coincide on a symmetric distribution and separate on a skewed one, where
$\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$ on right-skewed data because the mean follows the
tail. [[Mean]], [[Median]] and [[Mode]] carry the individual cases, and choosing which to
report is a decision about what the tail means.

[[Variance]] measures spread as the average squared distance from the centre. The sample
formula divides by $n - 1$:

$$
s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}
$$

On the data above that gives $4.57$, where dividing by $n$ gives $4.00$. The deviations are
taken from $\bar{x}$, which sits closer to this particular data than the unknown $\mu$ does,
so the squared deviations come out systematically too small. The $n - 1$ is the remaining
degrees of freedom and the correction that makes $s^2$ unbiased. The standard deviation
$s = 2.14$ carries the units of the data, so it is what gets reported, and the variance is
what algebra is done with. [[Descriptive Statistics]] covers the displays and the data
classification that comes before any of it.

### Probability

[[Probability]] covers sample spaces, events as [[Sets]], and three axioms:
$P(A) \geq 0$, $P(S) = 1$, and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ for disjoint events. Everything
else is derived from those, including $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$. Counting outcomes uses
[[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] from [[DISCRETE MATH]].

Mutually exclusive and independent describe opposite situations, and the words get confused
constantly. Two disjoint events with non-zero probability are maximally dependent, because one
occurring settles that the other did not.

[[Conditional Probability]] defines $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$, narrowing the sample
space to the cases where $B$ happened. Independence is exactly $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$, meaning
knowing $B$ changes nothing.

[[Bayes Theorem]] inverts the conditional, which is what turns a test result into a belief:

$$
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}
$$

```
A disease affects 1% of people.
The test catches 99% of cases and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people.
Someone tests positive. What is the chance they are ill?

P(positive) = (0.01)(0.99) + (0.99)(0.05) = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594
P(ill | positive) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 0.167
```

One positive test in six is a real case. The test is accurate and the answer is still mostly
false positives, because the 99% of healthy people are a much larger group and 5% of them is
larger than all of the sick. The base rate decides the answer, and ignoring it is the standard
error in reading a medical or a security alert.

### Random variables and distributions

A [[Random Variable]] attaches a number to an outcome, which is what makes arithmetic
possible. Expectation is the long-run average, $E[X] = \sum x_i P(x_i)$ in the discrete case
and $\int x f(x)\,dx$ in the continuous one. A fair die has $E[X] = 3.5$, a value it never
rolls, which is the first sign that an expectation describes the process and not any single
outcome. Expectation is linear unconditionally, so $E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b$.

Variance is $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$ and scales as
$\text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\text{Var}(X)$, so adding a constant shifts the centre and leaves the
spread alone. Variances add across independent variables and standard deviations do not, which
is why combining uncertainties means adding squares.

[[Probability Distribution]] is the family-selection table, and picking the right family is
most of the applied work:

| Distribution | Use when counting |
|---|---|
| [[Bernoulli Distribution]] | one trial with two outcomes |
| Binomial | successes in $n$ fixed trials, $\mu = np$, $\sigma^2 = np(1-p)$ |
| Poisson | events in an interval, identified by $\mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda$ |
| Geometric | trials until the first success |
| Exponential | waiting time until an event, the continuous geometric |
| Normal | a sum or average of many small effects |

[[Probability Density Function]] covers the continuous case, where $P(X = x) = 0$ for every
single value, since a point has no width. Only the integral over an interval is a probability,
which is why $<$ and $\leq$ give the same answer and why
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx = 1$ is the condition for a density to be legitimate. The CDF
$F(x) = P(X \leq x)$ is the antiderivative of the density, giving
$P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a)$, and every table lookup in the course is a CDF.

[[Normal Distribution]] is the bell curve, and standardising converts any normal to the
standard one:

$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

An IQ of 130 with $\mu = 100$ and $\sigma = 15$ gives $z = 2$, meaning two standard deviations
above the mean, and the 68-95-99.7 rule puts roughly 2.5% of people above it. Every normal
table in existence is one table because of that conversion.

### From one sample to every sample

[[Sampling Distribution]] is the idea the second half of the course rests on. A statistic such
as $\bar{x}$ is itself a random variable, because a different sample would have produced a
different value, and it has its own distribution across all possible samples.

The [[Central Limit Theorem]] describes that distribution: $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal
with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, whatever shape the population has.
The population can be skewed, bimodal or discrete, and the sample means are still normal for
$n$ around 30 or more. That is what allows one procedure to handle populations nobody has
measured.

The $\sqrt{n}$ is the practical consequence:

```
σ = 10, n = 25   ->  standard error = 10/5  = 2.0
σ = 10, n = 100  ->  standard error = 10/10 = 1.0
```

Halving the uncertainty took four times the data, so precision costs quadratically. That
formula decides how large a study has to be, and it is the most useful line in the course.

[[Confidence Interval]] turns the standard error into a range, using $z$ when $\sigma$ is
known and $t$ when it is estimated by $s$, where the $t$ distribution has fatter tails to pay
for that estimate and approaches $z$ as $n$ grows. The phrase 95% confident describes the
procedure: 95% of intervals built this way contain $\mu$, and this particular interval either
contains it or does not.

### Testing a claim

[[Hypothesis Testing]] sets up $H_0$ as the claim of no effect, computes a test statistic
measuring how far the data sits from what $H_0$ predicts, and compares the result against a
significance level $\alpha$ chosen before the data is examined. The structure is
[[Proof By Contradiction]] with a probability attached: assume $H_0$, derive that the observed
data would be unlikely, and reject the assumption.

A test rejects $H_0$ or fails to reject it, and never accepts it, because a failure to detect
an effect is consistent with the effect being small and with the sample being small.

[[P-VALUES]] is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, a probability of the data given the
hypothesis. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and it says nothing about the size
of the effect, so a tiny effect measured on a huge sample produces a small $p$-value and no
practical significance.

[[Type I and Type II Errors]] names the two ways a test fails, and the pair is the same object
the machine learning courses call a [[Confusion Matrix]]:

```
                    H₀ is true          H₀ is false
reject H₀           Type I error        correct
                    rate α              power = 1 - β
fail to reject      correct             Type II error, rate β
```

Lowering $\alpha$ raises $\beta$ at fixed $n$, since demanding stronger evidence means missing
more real effects. Lowering both requires more data. Power is $1 - \beta$, the probability of
detecting a real effect, which is the same quantity [[Sensitivity|recall]] measures in a
classifier.

### Categorical data and several means

[[Chi-Square Test]] compares observed counts against expected ones:

$$
\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}
$$

Goodness of fit compares one variable against a claimed distribution, which is how a
cryptanalyst scores a candidate decryption against English letter frequencies. A contingency
table tests two categorical variables for independence, with
$E_{ij} = \text{(row total)}\times\text{(column total)}/n$, which is the expected count if the
variables were unrelated. A $2 \times 2$ contingency table holds the same four counts as a
binary confusion matrix, with one tested for independence and the other summarised into
rates.

[[ANOVA]] compares three or more means in one test. Running $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise tests
inflates the family-wise error rate, since twenty tests at $\alpha = 0.05$ produce a false
positive about once by chance. The statistic is
$F = \text{MS}_{\text{between}} / \text{MS}_{\text{within}}$, a ratio comparing the spread
between group means against the spread inside the groups, and the sums of squares decompose as
$\text{SS}_{\text{total}} = \text{SS}_{\text{between}} + \text{SS}_{\text{within}}$.

### Regression

[[Linear Regression]] fits a line through a scatter of points by minimising the sum of squared
residuals:

$$
\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x, \qquad
\beta_1 = r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad
\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}
$$

The second formula forces the line through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, so the fit always passes
through the centre of the data. Residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with $x$ by
construction, which is why a visible pattern in a residual plot indicates the wrong model: the
fitting procedure already removed everything linear, so anything left with structure is
structure the line cannot represent.

[[Correlation]] covers Pearson's $r$, bounded by $-1$ and $1$, measuring linear association
alone. A perfect parabola through the origin gives $r = 0$, because the upward and downward
halves cancel. The coefficient of determination $r^2$ is the proportion of variance in $y$ the
line accounts for. Correlation is destroyed by non-linearity, inflated by outliers, reversible
by aggregating groups, and it establishes no causal claim.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]] supplies the probability foundations. Events are [[Sets]], the
  axioms are stated on sets, and [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] count the outcomes in the
  numerator.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] supplies continuous random variables, where a density is a
  function, a probability is an [[Integral]] of it, and the CDF is its antiderivative.
  [[CALCULUS 2]] supplies the integration techniques that evaluate the exponential and gamma
  cases.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] holds [[Least Squares]], which is
  [[Linear Regression]] derived a second way. Minimising the sum of squared residuals and
  taking a [[Projection]] onto a column space produce identical normal equations, and $r^2$ is
  Pythagoras on the resulting right triangle.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] rest on this course.
  [[Type I and Type II Errors]] supplies [[False Positive]] and [[False Negative]], power is
  [[Sensitivity]], the true negative rate is [[Specificity]], the contingency table is the
  [[Confusion Matrix]], and stratified sampling is [[Stratification]]. [[Logistic Regression]]
  handles a [[Binary Classification|binary label]], and [[Gradient Descent]] reaches the same
  line the normal equations produce in closed form.
- [[Information Theory]] defines [[Shannon Entropy]] as $-E[\log P(X)]$, an expectation of a
  [[Random Variable]], and [[Cross-Entropy]], [[KL Divergence]] and [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] are
  all functionals of a [[Probability Distribution]].
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] discusses collisions in [[Hashing]] without computing
  their likelihood. How many keys make a collision likely is the birthday problem, and average
  bucket occupancy is a Poisson question.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] treats average-case analysis as an expectation over the input
  distribution, which is where randomised quicksort's expected $O(n\log n)$ against its
  $O(n^2)$ worst case comes from. [[Random Numbers]] and [[Simulation]] in
  [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] sample distributions that resist integration.
- [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] uses frequency statistics for classical cryptanalysis, where
  the $\chi^2$ test above ranks candidate keys, and judges modern ciphers by whether their
  output is distinguishable from [[Random Numbers|uniform random]] data.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] evaluates joint densities with double integrals, and
  the normalising constant of the bell curve is the Gaussian integral, computed by the change
  to polar coordinates that this course quotes.
- [[CLASSICAL PHYSICS 1]] applies this in the laboratory, where
  [[Measurement Uncertainty]] propagates through a calculation and repeated readings scatter
  according to the [[Normal Distribution]].
- [[DIRECTED READING]] applies it to market data, where [[Volatility]] is
  [[Variance]] on a return series and [[Annualisation]] is the $\sqrt{n}$ scaling from the
  [[Central Limit Theorem]] used in the opposite direction.
